meta.headline: Every leap second has been an addition, never a subtraction
meta.seoTitle: Has a leap second ever been taken away?

dek.text: Has a leap second ever been taken away? The IERS record says no.

assertions.text: Every leap second since UTC began in 1972 has been added to civil time; none has ever been taken away: the IERS table of TAI-UTC runs from 10 seconds on 1 January 1972 to 37 seconds on 1 January 2017, each value one second larger than the last, 27 steps in all.

description.text: Every leap second so far was an addition, never a subtraction.

assertions.text: Every leap second since UTC began in 1972 has been added to civil time; none has ever been taken away: the IERS table of TAI-UTC runs from 10 seconds on 1 January 1972 to 37 seconds on 1 January 2017, each value one second larger than the last, 27 steps in all.

sections.name: answer
sections.heading: Every step in the record added a second

sentences.text: The IERS table records the gap between atomic and civil time, and it has only ever widened.

assertions.text: Every leap second since UTC began in 1972 has been added to civil time; none has ever been taken away: the IERS table of TAI-UTC runs from 10 seconds on 1 January 1972 to 37 seconds on 1 January 2017, each value one second larger than the last, 27 steps in all.

sentences.text: All twenty-seven steps added a second.
sentences.note: The table's opening and closing figures are the size of the gap between atomic and civil time, not a count of leap seconds: the 27 steps between 10 seconds and 37 seconds are the leap seconds, and the figure block carries all three figures with their cite.
